Yet this second outing — a follow-up to Weejuns (2023) — doesn't quite match the vitality of its predecessor, often feeling emotionally distant and strangely restrained. Berlin-based NNHMN have built their recent work around movement, tension, and transformation. With “Opera of Lust and The Art of Sorrow”, the duo continue to expand a sound that connects darkwave, electronic body music, performance, and club discipline without reducing itself to nostalgia. As “Cold Like Steel” prepares to open a slower, more melancholic side of the project, Lee and Michal speak about theatrical writing, genre evolution, live tension, Grauzone 2026, and “UNTERWELT”, their Halloween event at Festsaal Kreuzberg in Berlin.

Nearly five years after his debut album Altitude (BASE Records, 2020), Chicago trumpeter Connor Bernhard gathered most of that album's cohorts for his second recording as a leader, Pathways. What also returns is the same bright, engaging horn that distinguishes Bernhard and lifts the proceedings significantly. His band—the three repeaters Julius Tucker on piano, Jeff Swanson on guitar, and Clif Wallace on drums, joined by Evan Salvacion Levine on bass—follows through with their own engaging support.

When four hands meet across 176 keys, is it even possible for pianists to check their egos at the stage door? Piano duets, by their very nature, often invite comparison—even confrontation. Consider the 1977 encounter between Mary Lou Williams and Cecil Taylor, the high-profile 1978 concerts by Herbie Hancock and Chick Corea, or Kris Davis and Craig Taborn's Octopus (Pyroclastic, 2018). Each of these pairings carried the tension of a musical grappling match. Even Bill Evans' overdubbed Conversations with Myself (Verve, 1963) suggested an internal struggle. If that competitive impulse is the norm, then Katarahi by Satoko Fujii and Myra Melford stands as a striking exception.

Listening to the February 2026 digital release of Trudy Lynn's Turning the Same Ole Corners inspires a trip back in time to the Consumer Electronics Show at McCormick Place, Chicago, where Sony unveiled its first CD player. The sound was clean, crystalline, futuristic. Great for classical. Great for pop. But for blues—the music of roadhouse sweat, smoke and booze—it always felt like someone had wiped down the bar with antiseptic. That tension between polish and grit hangs over this 2026 reissue, originally released in 2002 as Memories of You.

Between the Air, their latest and eighth album, exemplifies this spirit of experimentation. The album of musical extremes foregrounds texture, using many extended techniques and the full spectrum of timbres and pitches possible on the mixed-quintet's instruments. But while much of Between the Air explores the unruliness of sound, its power lies in how each work colors silence with the understated nature of air itself.

excerpt: During the 1970s French singer and entertainer Sacha Distel performed a number of times at the London Palladium and on British TV. Long since deleted, it was a collectors' piece. Barney Wilen makes himself known from the off with a strong solo. John Lewis directs well from the front. An excellent reissue.

Pianist McCoy Tyner didn't let his path falter after the years with John Coltrane, continuing with powerful, high energy hard bop, his piano style full of blocked chords and melodic runs. From a live performance at the Umbria Jazz Festival in 1993.

There are times when clarinet-wielding Anat Cohen seems to have invaded and taken up residence in locations normally occupied by the saxophone. But she allows the clarinet to maintain and extend its character in her celebrated foursome Quartetinho by establishing a chamber-jazz format.

Jazz pianists overburdened with a classical technique can do the music a disservice. A bass player with one, who has performed in a symphony orchestra, may be better placed to experiment with mixing genres. On this often mesmerising album Mark Wade reimagines inspiring music from the concert platform.

With many of its original recordings lost to history, it's up to a new generation to revive the art form. The scene report covers the Belgian folk revival through artists like Wouter Vandenabeele, Tom Theuns, Avalanche Kaito, Didier Laloy, Tcha Limberger, and labels like homerecords.be, exploring how musicians are breathing new life into traditional forms.

In a musical landscape where virtually every new title promoted as 'jazz' would be unrecognizable to the musicians who actually created it, circa 1895, in New Orleans, it's refreshing to encounter a new release that not only acknowledges those pioneers but also respects and honours them.

Veteran French bassist Henri Texier is calling on past compositions of his to be applied as balm to brows fevered by the current anxiety-provoking atmosphere. Octogenarian Texier has been in the music business for six decades. The vitality of Healing Songs testifies to music as continuously inspirational.

This is a vinyl reissue of bass player Buster Williams' debut album as a leader, originally released on Muse in 1975, in which the concept is very much of the day, taking its lead from the 'electrified' atmosphere of Miles Davis's In A Silent Way and Bitches Brew.

Some detect a Nordic influence in Lilly Hertzman's new album Heartshaped, but it is more reminiscent of Joni Mitchell's more jazz-influenced years. Poetic lyrics, strong melodies but with sophisticated changes, jazzy arrangements and some of the best international players you can find.

The Italian duo B.I.T., made up of pianist Manuela Pasqui and saxophonist Danielle Di Majo, go to great pains to explain that their latest CD R-Esistenze is about resistance - the resistance movement during WWII and women's struggle for emancipation.

album: Elina Duni, Rob Luft: Reaching For The Moon
excerpt: Albanian-born singer Elina Duni is now on her sixth ECM recording, her third with British guitarist Rob Luft, this time just as a duo. She draws on a wide variety of languages and genres, covering traditional pieces, a Persian lullaby, an Italian ballad, Gabriel Faure's art song, all bookended by Irving Berlin's title song and Ornette Coleman's Lonely Woman.

album: Ahmad Jamal: At The Jazz Showcase, Live In Chicago
excerpt: In March 1976 Ahmad Jamal and his trio performed at the Jazz Showcase in Chicago. Everything Jamal plays here is beautifully delivered. Best of all is the concluding 21-minute Swahililand, a Jamal composition previewed in 1974 which manages to combine a whirl of profound pianisms alongside references to the English carol God Rest Ye Merry, Gentlemen.

Modha released their debut album Through The Cycle in 2023 and have now recorded their second offering. They remain in their tranquil soundscape, capturing the energy of live studio sessions and natural imperfections while retaining polished production. The Berlin-based jazz duo consists of Dhanya Langer and Max Scholl.
